title: Why the Navy Painted Ships Black
topic: Why the British Royal Navy painted the hulls of its ships black in the early 18th century (to conceal biofouling and improve speed)

lines: A young carpenter slathers tar on a brand‑new hull, his hands trembling.
His mates snicker, saying the black paint is just for looks.
Weeks later, the ship drifts slower, its wake thick with slime.
The crew grumbles as the voyage takes longer than promised.
You see, it’s like trying to run in a wet sweater – the extra drag hurts.
The black mixture of tar and pitch actually seals the wood, hiding barnacles and algae.
By hiding biofouling, the hull stays smooth and the ship keeps its speed.
Ironically, the very darkness that made the ships look menacing was a simple speed hack.

claims.claim: Biofouling can increase hull drag up to sixty percent, reducing speed by ten percent and requiring up to forty percent more fuel.
Before the eighteenth century, ships were coated with "Black stuff" – a mixture of tar and pitch – to protect the hull.
